paragraphs: Autonomous controllers must pursue useful goals while staying within safe operating conditions. These objectives can compete: a controller that prioritizes performance may accept unsafe behavior, while a strongly protective controller may act too conservatively. This paper brings both objectives into a single optimal control problem, representing performance through a cost function and safety through explicit constraints on the system’s state.

The authors show that the resulting value function satisfies a Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation. This function describes the best achievable cost within the constrained problem. Their physics-informed learning framework approximates it efficiently, using the governing mathematical structure to guide learning.

Approximation introduces errors, so the framework also includes verification based on conformal prediction. This quantifies learning error to obtain a safety value function with high confidence and a probabilistic bound on performance degradation. Case studies demonstrate learning safe, effective controllers for complex, high-dimensional systems. The practical contribution is the combination of constrained control, scalable approximation, and quantified uncertainty; the learned safety assurances retain the stated high-confidence qualification.
icml-2025-a-physics-informed-machine-lea.tldr: The framework combines constrained optimal control, physics-informed learning, and conformal verification to learn controllers with high-confidence safety and quantified performance error.

paragraphs: Speculative decoding accelerates language generation by using a draft model to propose tokens and a target model to process multiple proposals in one forward pass. A practical obstacle is that existing approaches require both models to use the same vocabulary. That restriction narrows the available draft models and can make training a compatible model necessary.

This paper introduces three algorithms that remove the shared-vocabulary requirement. They work with existing models without additional training or modifications. All three preserve the target model’s output distribution, which is the meaning of lossless here: acceleration does not replace the target’s distribution with an approximation supplied by the drafter.

Experiments cover summarization, programming, and long-context tasks, with reported speedups reaching 2.8 times standard autoregressive decoding. That figure is an observed maximum across the evaluations. The broader contribution is flexibility in model pairing: removing vocabulary compatibility as a requirement substantially expands the pool of usable drafters and makes speculative decoding easier to apply without a separate training effort.
icml-2025-accelerating-llm-inference-wit.tldr: Three lossless speculative decoding algorithms allow different draft and target vocabularies, achieving speedups of up to 2.8 times without retraining.

paragraphs: Collaborative learning lets participants train a shared model by exchanging focused updates while keeping their data local. Participation raises a reward question: how should someone who contributes more receive a correspondingly better outcome? Aequa studies allocation of model rewards, where participants receive final models with different performance levels based on their contributions.

The approach uses a slimmable neural network, a shared model that can operate at different widths. Its performance is designed to decline gradually as width decreases. This gives the allocation procedure a way to adjust the model each participant receives while drawing those rewards from one collaboratively trained global model.

A post-training algorithm chooses each participant’s model width according to their contribution. The authors study convergence theoretically and evaluate the approach across datasets and architectures. They also extend allocation to occur during training. The paper focuses on turning contribution information into differentiated model access; contribution assessment is a separate part of the broader fairness problem. Its central idea is to make model width a practical control for distributing performance-based rewards.
icml-2025-aequa-fair-model-rewards-in-co.tldr: Aequa uses adjustable-width shared networks to allocate model rewards whose performance reflects participants’ contributions to collaborative learning.

paragraphs: Learning a ranking from human feedback is difficult when people can compare only a small fraction of the available items. This paper asks which groups of items should be presented for comparison so that a limited feedback budget produces as few ranking mistakes as possible. It models preferences with a Plackett–Luce model and considers comparisons involving K items drawn from a universe of N.

The authors choose comparisons using D-optimal design, which minimizes worst-case ranking loss under the estimated preference model. The computational difficulty is the enormous number of candidate subsets: considering all possible groups becomes infeasible in the setting studied. Selecting informative feedback therefore requires an efficient optimization method as well as a statistical objective.

Their solution is a randomized Frank–Wolfe algorithm using memoization and sparse updates. These techniques reuse computations and limit update work, giving a per-iteration complexity of O(N² + K²). The paper analyzes the algorithm and reports empirical superiority on synthetic and open-source language datasets. The result connects selective feedback collection with a computationally manageable way to optimize which comparisons to request.
icml-2025-comparing-few-to-rank-many-act.tldr: A randomized optimization algorithm efficiently selects informative item comparisons to improve preference rankings under a limited feedback budget.

paragraphs: Data assimilation repeatedly updates an estimate of a changing physical system using new observations. In nonlinear state space models, the uncertainty over the system’s state can have a complicated, non-Gaussian shape. Deep Bayesian Filtering addresses this difficulty by introducing latent variables alongside the physical variables and designing the latent model to support tractable uncertainty updates.

Two structural choices make this possible. State transitions in the latent space are constrained to be linear, and a learned inverse observation operator produces a Gaussian distribution over latent states from observations. Together, these choices ensure Gaussian posteriors in the constructed latent formulation, allowing recursive updates to be calculated analytically.

The model learns these operators and other latent parameters by maximizing an evidence lower bound. Because its recursive computation is analytical, it avoids accumulating Monte Carlo sampling errors across time steps. Experiments report better performance than existing methods in scenarios with highly non-Gaussian posteriors. The contribution is a structured learned representation that makes repeated Bayesian updating manageable even when uncertainty in the original physical problem is difficult.
icml-2025-deep-bayesian-filter-for-bayes.tldr: Deep Bayesian Filtering learns a structured latent model that enables analytical uncertainty updates for nonlinear systems with complex physical-state posteriors.

paragraphs: Concept-based explanations investigate whether a neural network responds to meaningful visual ideas, such as stripes when recognizing a zebra. Building these explanations normally requires practitioners to propose concepts and collect image sets representing them. That manual process takes effort and can overlook concepts that matter to the model but are difficult to anticipate or illustrate.

This paper treats the creation of concept image sets as an image generation task. A practitioner supplies an approximate textual description, and a vision-language generative model is adapted to produce useful examples. The authors find that simply using a standard generator does not yield meaningful concepts, motivating a reinforcement learning-based preference optimization algorithm for fine-tuning.

Experiments demonstrate that the method can efficiently and reliably express diverse concepts, including ones that are challenging to construct manually. Its contribution is to improve the material used for concept-based investigation: generated image sets make otherwise laborious concepts easier to examine. The work therefore connects generative modeling with post-hoc explanation, using preference learning to make generated images more suitable for understanding internal representations.
icml-2025-explainable-concept-generation.tldr: Preference-tuned vision-language generation creates concept image sets that help explain neural representations with less manual collection.

paragraphs: Physical systems involving force exchange and energy dissipation are difficult to learn because their behavior reflects both geometric constraints and energy transfer. Geometric Contact Flows incorporates Riemannian and contact geometry into the learning framework. These mathematical structures act as inductive biases, shaping the kinds of dynamics the model can represent.

The method first builds a latent contact Hamiltonian model with desirable properties, such as stability or energy conservation. An ensemble of contactomorphisms then adapts that model to the target dynamics while preserving the encoded properties. The central idea is to build useful physical structure into an initial model and use transformations that retain it during adaptation.

The ensemble also supports uncertainty-aware geodesics, geometric paths that draw the system’s behavior toward regions supported by the data. This mechanism is intended to support robust generalization and adaptation to unseen scenarios. Experiments on physical-system dynamics and robotic interaction control demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness. The paper combines property-preserving transformations with uncertainty-sensitive behavior, addressing how a learned dynamical model can adapt while retaining chosen structural commitments.
icml-2025-geometric-contact-flows-contac.tldr: Geometric Contact Flows learns physical dynamics through geometry-preserving transformations that retain chosen properties and support uncertainty-aware adaptation.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning must share useful information across clients whose data distributions differ. Bayesian approaches represent each client’s model parameters with a personalized posterior distribution, then combine information into a global distribution. The paper identifies heuristic aggregation as a source of strong bias that can undermine the global model’s generalization.

The proposed framework makes local personalization and global aggregation parts of one hierarchical Bayesian inference problem. It places a conjugate hyper-prior over the parameters of the personalized posteriors. This additional probabilistic layer allows the method to jointly compute a global posterior for aggregation and local posteriors for individual clients.

That hierarchy provides a principled way to share statistical information while retaining differences among clients. Extensive empirical evaluation reports state-of-the-art performance, attributed to this balance between local distinctiveness and global robustness. The authors also show that existing Bayesian personalized federated learning methods arise as special cases of their framework. The contribution therefore includes both a learning approach and a broader mathematical account of how related methods connect.
icml-2025-harnessing-heterogeneous-stati.tldr: A hierarchical Bayesian framework jointly learns global and personalized posteriors to share information across clients with different data distributions.

paragraphs: Third-party language model inference raises a privacy question: can an outside service recover a user’s text from internal model representations? This paper introduces a reconstruction technique that recovers original prompts from hidden states with nearly perfect accuracy across multiple leading models in the open-weights setting. The findings show that exposing these representations can reveal substantially more than their indirect form might suggest.

The attack remains effective against several permutation-based and noise-based defenses. This challenges the security assumptions behind previously proposed schemes that rely on such transformations. The authors describe the reconstruction method as conceptually simple while reporting that its practical effectiveness had not previously been established to their knowledge.

To address the vulnerability, they propose Cascade, a multi-party inference scheme that shards computation along the sequence dimension to protect user input. Theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation support its security against the new attack and earlier methods, while retaining computational and communication efficiency. The paper thus pairs evidence of a concrete privacy weakness with a defense evaluated against the attack methods considered.
icml-2025-hidden-no-more-attacking-and-d.tldr: The paper demonstrates highly accurate prompt reconstruction from hidden states and introduces Cascade, a multi-party defense evaluated against this and prior attacks.

paragraphs: Pseudo-random sequences can look irregular while following a precise rule. This paper studies whether Transformers can learn sequences generated by repeatedly multiplying a number, adding a constant, and taking the remainder modulo m. With sufficient model capacity and training-data variety, the authors find in-context prediction can extend to generator parameters and moduli absent from training.

When the modulus is fixed but the multiplier and additive constant are unseen, successful learning reaches moduli of 2³². Analysis of embeddings and attention indicates that models learn to factorize the modulus and represent numbers digit by digit. These internal structures help explain how sequential prediction becomes possible despite the apparent randomness.

With unseen moduli, models generalize up to test moduli of 2¹⁶. Here the observed strategy has two stages: estimate the modulus from context, then use prime factorizations to predict. Accuracy changes sharply at depth three in this task, and the context length needed for high accuracy grows sublinearly with the modulus. These are findings about the studied generator family and training conditions, revealing specific algorithmic structures learned by Transformers.
icml-2025-how-can-transformers-predict-p.tldr: With sufficient capacity and training variety, Transformers learn algorithmic structures that predict linear congruential sequences with unseen parameters and moduli.

paragraphs: Medical image segmentation models can struggle when images come from domains different from those used for training. LangDAug addresses this problem through data augmentation for multi-source generalization in two-dimensional segmentation. Its aim is to enrich training with samples connecting the available source domains, giving the model a broader range of image variation to learn from.

The method trains energy-based models using contrastive divergence, then uses Langevin dynamics to move between source domains and generate intermediate samples. This makes augmentation a learned process for exploring relationships among domains. The generated examples provide the segmentation model with training variation derived from those relationships.

The theoretical analysis shows a regularization effect. For generalized linear models specifically, it bounds Rademacher complexity using the intrinsic dimensionality of the data manifold, connecting the analysis to underlying data structure. Experiments on fundus and two-dimensional prostate MRI segmentation report better performance than state-of-the-art domain generalization methods. LangDAug also complements existing domain-randomization approaches, suggesting that intermediate-domain sampling can provide useful variation alongside other augmentation strategies.
icml-2025-langdaug-langevin-data-augment.tldr: LangDAug generates intermediate-domain medical images with Langevin dynamics to improve segmentation generalization across domains.

paragraphs: Neural operators learn solution mappings for partial differential equations from data, offering a route to faster prediction than numerical methods. Existing approaches can become computationally expensive in high-dimensional settings and struggle to capture continuous or long-range relationships in evolving physical systems. The Latent Mamba Operator, or LaMO, targets these modeling and scalability challenges.

LaMO combines state-space models operating in a latent representation with the kernel integral formulation used by neural operators. The intended combination brings efficient state-space computation together with an expressive way to represent relationships across a physical domain. The authors also establish a theoretical connection between state-space models and neural-operator kernel integrals, providing a mathematical link between the components.

Experiments span solid and fluid physics, with data represented as regular grids, structured meshes, and point clouds. The paper reports consistent state-of-the-art performance and a 32.3% improvement over existing baselines in solution-operator approximation. These results support the proposed combination across the tested representations and PDE benchmarks, showing how latent state-space modeling can contribute to learning complex physical solution mappings.
icml-2025-latent-mamba-operator-for-part.tldr: LaMO combines latent state-space modeling with neural-operator kernels, reporting improved PDE solution approximation across varied physical datasets and representations.

paragraphs: Predicting future links in a changing graph requires useful representations of both structure and time. Fixed positional encodings may adapt poorly to complex attributed graphs, while learned encodings can still overlook evolving connections and features. L-STEP introduces a learnable spatial-temporal positional encoding designed to capture this changing information efficiently.

The authors prove that their positional learning scheme preserves graph properties from a spatial-temporal spectral perspective. They also show that multilayer perceptrons can exploit the resulting encoding and reach Transformer performance on it. This matters because dense or relational attention can be expensive on large graphs: a useful encoding can make simpler prediction machinery competitive.

Evaluation examines different initial positional encodings, theoretical complexity, and empirical runtime. L-STEP reports lower running time than state-of-the-art methods and superior temporal link prediction across 13 datasets against 10 algorithms, covering transductive and inductive settings with three sampling strategies. It also achieves leading performance on the large-scale TGB benchmark. Together, these findings support learning richer positional information as a route to both accurate and efficient temporal graph prediction.
icml-2025-learnable-spatial-temporal-pos.tldr: L-STEP learns spatial-temporal graph encodings that let simple multilayer perceptrons deliver strong, efficient temporal link prediction.

paragraphs: Choosing how much training data to draw from each source can substantially affect a model’s downstream usefulness. MixMin formulates this choice as a nested optimization problem: a mixture is good when training on it produces a model that performs well on the downstream objective. Directly solving that problem is generally intractable.

The authors observe that the mixture objective becomes convex as the model class grows larger. They develop a gradient-based method for optimizing this convex objective and test it on language modeling and chemistry. Across their experiments, MixMin is the only evaluated method that improves the mixture in every case.

For a Pythia-410M model trained on 8.2 billion tokens, mixture selection uses less than 0.2% additional compute and yields 1–5% relative improvement in negative log likelihood on four named evaluations. Mixtures selected for smaller models also improve larger-model training, suggesting possible scale invariance. In bioassay mixing for XGBoost, average precision improves by 0.03–0.15. These findings support efficient mixture selection while leaving scale invariance as a suggestion from the observed transfer.
icml-2025-mixmin-finding-data-mixtures-v.tldr: MixMin uses convex optimization to select training-data mixtures, improving language and chemistry results with low reported selection overhead.

paragraphs: Sparse variational Gaussian processes make posterior approximation tractable by introducing inducing variables. A conventional construction retains the prior’s conditional distribution over training function values given those variables. This paper shows that, for model training, this familiar restriction can be relaxed to obtain a more flexible variational distribution.

The new conditional distribution introduces one extra parameter per training example. For Gaussian process regression, the authors optimize the evidence lower bound analytically over these parameters. Eliminating them in this way produces a tractable collapsed bound that is tighter than the previous bound, so the added flexibility does not require leaving all those parameters in the numerical optimization.

The resulting objective supports stochastic optimization and needs only minor changes to existing sparse Gaussian process implementations. The paper also describes extensions to non-Gaussian likelihoods. Experiments on several datasets show that the method can reduce bias in learned hyperparameters and improve predictions. Its contribution is a better training bound obtained by reconsidering a standard approximation assumption, with empirical benefits expressed as possibilities demonstrated on the evaluated data.
icml-2025-new-bounds-for-sparse-variatio.tldr: Relaxing a standard variational assumption yields a tighter tractable training bound that can improve sparse Gaussian process hyperparameters and predictions.

paragraphs: Decentralized federated learning trains models collaboratively without a central server or exchanging raw data. A major difficulty is that participants’ data can follow different distributions, reflecting local environments and behaviors. NTK-DFL addresses this heterogeneity by adapting a neural tangent kernel approach, previously useful in centralized federated learning, to decentralized collaboration.

The proposed method combines neural tangent kernel-based model evolution with model averaging. Its defining feature is the interaction between these two components: differences among clients’ models are used to improve learning. In the authors’ account, this interaction improves both predictive accuracy and convergence when local datasets differ substantially.

Experiments report consistently higher accuracy than baselines in highly heterogeneous settings, where other approaches often struggle. The method also reaches target performance in 4.6 times fewer communication rounds. Evaluation spans multiple datasets, network topologies, and degrees of heterogeneity, supporting the approach across the tested decentralized conditions. The practical significance is that improving how differing client models interact can reduce the communication needed to achieve useful performance.
icml-2025-ntk-dfl-enhancing-decentralize.tldr: NTK-DFL combines neural tangent kernel updates with model averaging to improve decentralized learning accuracy and communication efficiency under heterogeneous data.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a language model to imitate a teacher, but the teacher is itself an imperfect representation of the desired distribution. This paper asks whether optimizing imitation too strongly can therefore harm the underlying objective. The authors call this teacher hacking, drawing a parallel with reward hacking during reinforcement learning from human feedback.

To make the distinction measurable, they construct a controlled chain of models. An oracle represents the ground-truth distribution, a teacher is distilled from that oracle, and a student is distilled from the teacher. This setup separates progress toward copying the teacher from progress toward matching the original source distribution.

In experiments with a fixed offline distillation dataset, teacher hacking occurs. The authors also detect its onset through deviations from polynomial convergence laws. Online data generation effectively mitigates the phenomenon, with data diversity identified as the key preventive factor in the studied setting. The results explain why better teacher imitation can become misleading and why the diversity of distillation data matters for retaining alignment with the underlying learning objective.
icml-2025-on-teacher-hacking-in-language.tldr: Controlled experiments show that fixed-data distillation can overfit an imperfect teacher, while diverse online data mitigates this teacher-hacking effect.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction expresses uncertainty through prediction sets with coverage guarantees. For outputs with several dimensions, reducing uncertainty to a single score can discard useful geometric structure. Some alternatives impose a predetermined convex shape, which may fit the actual uncertainty poorly. This paper develops a procedure that works directly with multivariate score functions.

The method uses optimal transport, specifically Monge–Kantorovich vector ranks and quantiles, to construct prediction regions. These regions can have flexible and potentially non-convex shapes. That flexibility allows the shape of the uncertainty region to better reflect complex patterns in the output space instead of following a fixed geometric template.

The authors prove finite-sample, distribution-free coverage properties comparable to standard conformal methods and adapt the procedure to multi-output regression and multiclass classification. They also propose adjustments giving adaptive regions with asymptotic conditional coverage guarantees. These are distinct guarantees: the conditional result is asymptotic. Practical regression and classification evaluations illustrate advantages in coverage and efficiency, supporting the value of retaining multivariate geometry when constructing uncertainty regions.
icml-2025-optimal-transport-based-confor.tldr: Optimal transport enables flexible multivariate conformal prediction regions with finite-sample coverage guarantees and asymptotic conditional guarantees for proposed adaptations.

paragraphs: Long-context language generation places heavy demands on the key-value cache, which stores information used during decoding. In the edge-device settings considered here, loading the full cache at each step is a major source of memory use and latency. QuantSpec targets this bottleneck within self-speculative decoding, where a draft model proposes tokens for the target model to evaluate.

The draft model shares the target model’s architecture but uses 4-bit weights and a hierarchical 4-bit quantized key-value cache. This makes reduced numerical precision central to accelerating draft generation. The design aims to lower the cost of proposing tokens while keeping enough agreement with the target for proposals to be accepted frequently.

The paper reports acceptance rates above 90% and consistent end-to-end acceleration reaching approximately 2.5 times. It outperforms other self-speculative approaches that use sparse key-value caches for long-context inference and reduces memory requirements by approximately a factor of 1.3 relative to those alternatives. These findings show that cache representation and draft acceptance must work together for speculative generation to deliver practical gains.
icml-2025-quantspec-self-speculative-dec.tldr: QuantSpec uses 4-bit draft weights and a hierarchical quantized cache to accelerate long-context decoding while maintaining acceptance rates above 90%.

paragraphs: Tracking several objects in three dimensions is an important part of autonomous-driving perception. End-to-end query-based trackers detect objects and follow them over time, but difficult cases such as occlusion and small targets remain challenging. S2-Track organizes this tracking process into three parts—query initialization, propagation, and matching—and improves each part within one framework.

For initialization, predicted two-dimensional object information and depth provide an initial estimate of an object’s three-dimensional location. For propagation, an uncertainty-aware probabilistic decoder uses probabilistic attention to capture uncertainty in object predictions. For matching, hierarchical query denoising improves training robustness and convergence. The improvements address how tracking hypotheses begin, evolve, and are matched.

On the nuScenes test split, S2-Track reports 66.3% AMOTA, exceeding the previous best end-to-end solution by the stated margin of 8.9% AMOTA. The paper also reports first place on the tracking leaderboard. These results support a systematic approach to improving the tracker’s constituent stages, with the benchmark gains demonstrating the effectiveness of their combined design.
icml-2025-s2-track-a-simple-yet-strong-a.tldr: S2-Track improves query initialization, uncertainty-aware propagation, and matching to achieve leading reported nuScenes 3D tracking performance.

paragraphs: Generating code from natural language requires a model to keep the user’s requirements relevant throughout generation. This paper observes that language models tend to devote less attention to the prompt as they produce more code tokens. The authors hypothesize that this attention dilution is an important contributor to code-generation errors.

Selective Prompt Anchoring, or SPA, is designed to guide code models back toward the user’s intent during generation. Its focus is the connection between the growing code output and the original request. The motivating distinction is between the measured decline in prompt attention and the proposed explanation that this decline contributes to incorrect code.

The authors evaluate SPA with six base language models across six benchmarks. They report Pass@1 improvements of up to 12.9% and consistent superiority over state-of-the-art code-generation methods in all evaluated settings. Pass@1 concerns success from a single generated attempt, so the result speaks to the usefulness of the first answer. The experiments support prompt anchoring as an effective intervention while the causal explanation remains framed as the authors’ hypothesis.
icml-2025-selective-prompt-anchoring-for.tldr: Selective Prompt Anchoring reinforces attention to user intent during code generation, improving Pass@1 by up to 12.9% in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Modeling several interacting solids requires tracking how each body deforms and how its interactions affect other bodies. Existing deep learning methods often learn these influences implicitly. As the number of solids grows, the paper argues that this can make complex physical interactions difficult to capture accurately, especially when different systems have different coupling patterns.

Unisoma introduces a Transformer-based model with explicit modules for factors influencing deformation. Contact modules and an adaptive interaction allocation mechanism directly represent physical interactions, while a triplet relationship is used to learn deformation. The model can handle variable numbers of solids, making the same framework applicable to systems with different compositions.

The purpose of this structure is to give each solid detailed treatment while reducing confusion from blending information across bodies. Experiments report consistent state-of-the-art performance across seven established datasets and two complex multi-solid tasks. The findings support explicit organization of interactions as a useful alternative to leaving all interaction structure implicit, particularly for the diverse coupling patterns encountered in the evaluated multi-solid systems.
icml-2025-unisoma-a-unified-transformer-.tldr: Unisoma explicitly models contact and interaction structure to predict deformation in systems containing variable numbers of solids.

paragraphs: Understanding a single neural network does not automatically reveal how its concepts correspond to those of another network. Universal Sparse Autoencoders address this comparison problem by learning one concept space shared across multiple pretrained models. The aim is to reconstruct and interpret their internal activations within a common representation.

The framework trains a single overcomplete sparse autoencoder that can take activations from any model under consideration and decode them into approximate activations of another. A shared training objective encourages its dictionary to capture common factors of variation across architectures, tasks, and datasets. Cross-model reconstruction therefore provides a basis for aligning concepts rather than analyzing each network entirely separately.

In vision models, the authors find semantically coherent and important shared concepts ranging from colors and textures to parts and objects. They also identify applications such as coordinated activation maximization. The contribution is a framework for interpretable comparison across the models being studied: a common concept dictionary makes it possible to investigate representational correspondences at several levels of visual abstraction.
icml-2025-universal-sparse-autoencoders-.tldr: Universal Sparse Autoencoders learn a shared interpretable concept space by reconstructing activations across multiple pretrained models.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how language models might help reduce the environmental impact of food systems. The authors develop a typology of design and prediction tasks using sustainable-food research and domain-expert input, then evaluate six language models on four tasks. This task-based approach examines where assistance is useful and where difficult tradeoffs remain.

For sustainable protein design, food scientists estimate that collaboration with a language model could reduce time spent by 45% on average, compared with 22% for collaboration with another expert. These are expert estimates. For menu design, however, language models produce suboptimal solutions when asked to balance human satisfaction with climate impact.

The authors respond with a framework combining language models and combinatorial optimization. In a hypothetical restaurant setting, their approach reduces emissions associated with food choices by 79% while maintaining participants’ satisfaction with their available choices. The results indicate potential for language models to assist sustainable food development, with optimization providing support when choices require balancing competing objectives. The emissions finding retains its hypothetical-restaurant scope.
icml-2025-what-can-large-language-models.tldr: Language models show promise for sustainable food design, while combining them with optimization improves menu tradeoffs in a hypothetical restaurant setting.

paragraphs: Keeping a language model’s factual knowledge current can require costly retraining. Knowledge editing offers another route, but evaluations based on small or synthetic collections of edits provide limited evidence about repeated updates at practical scale. WikiBigEdit introduces a benchmark intended to bring lifelong knowledge editing closer to the volume and character of real factual changes.

The benchmark is built from real-world Wikidata edits and initially contains more than 500,000 question-answer pairs for knowledge editing. It includes a comprehensive evaluation pipeline and is designed to extend automatically as further edits become available. This continuing construction supports evaluation of methods intended to incorporate knowledge over time.

The authors use WikiBigEdit to examine existing editing techniques under large volumes of real facts. They also compare them with retrieval augmentation and continual fine-tuning, broadening the assessment beyond specialized editing methods. The contribution is an evaluation resource and comparative study of practical updating capabilities. The supplied account establishes the scale and design of that investigation without reporting a specific winning technique or numerical performance conclusion.
icml-2025-wikibigedit-understanding-the-.tldr: WikiBigEdit provides over 500,000 real-world knowledge-editing question-answer pairs and an extensible pipeline for evaluating repeated factual updates at scale.
